newsitem.title: USA: Staples merger would raise prices.
newsitem.headline: Staples merger would raise prices.

text.p: A government expert told a U.S. District Court Tuesday that a $4 billion merger between office superstores Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. would raise prices to consumers by 5 percent to 10 percent.

"Even after taking into account the potential for efficiencies, this merger can be expected to lead to a large and significant increase in the price of office supplies," testified Frederick Warren-Boulton, who was retained by the Federal Trade Commission.
He said the probable price increase was "about 6 percent ... 5 percent to 10 percent is a safe range."

Boulton's testimony came on the second day of a five-day hearing to provide evidence for U.S. District Court Judge Thomas Hogan to decide whether to permit the merger, which was challenged as anticompetitive by a 3-2 vote of the FTC.

Warren-Boulton, a Princeton-trained economist who worked in the Justice Department as chief antitrust economist during the administration of President Reagan, said he had several kinds of evidence to back his findings.
Warren-Boulton, citing internal documents, said the office superstores were facing the problem of saturation in coming years.

In 1995, Office Depot, Staples and the third player, OfficeMax Inc., were in only 17 percent of the same cities, according to internal documents he cited. Staples' projections showed they expected that to jump to 69 percent by the year 2000, and that would mean tough competition, he said.

On Monday, the government offered charts based on internal Staples and Office Depot documents showing prices were lower in cities with two or three competing office superstores than in cities with just one.

"It's a classic example of confusion between correlation and causation," Staples attorney Don Kempf said Monday. He presented his own chart showing price differences in office superstores, depending on whether they were located in cities whose names ended in vowels or ended in consonants.
But the FTC's Warren-Boulton testified Tuesday that underlying economic theory gave meaning to the correlations.
An FTC spokesman said that underlying, classic antitrust theory is that economic concentration leads to higher prices.
Warren-Boulton was the fourth witness brought by the FTC. The FTC has also presented witnesses from Kmart Corp., BJ's Wholesale Club and Computer City.
Representatives from the stores testified that they sold some of the same products as Staples and Office Depot, but that they were in very different businesses.
Warren-Boulton buttressed that perspective by likening the office superstores to grocery supermarkets -- the industry which he said gave birth to the idea of office superstores.

Warren-Boulton said while he might shop for groceries at warehouse discounter Price-Costco, convenience stores and small independent groceries as well as Safeway and its Washington regional competitor, Giant, the two supermarkets were in a category by themselves.
He said the existence of the other stores would not justify permitting the merger of Safeway and Giant.
Judge Hogan has said he will rule on the case by mid-June.
